samples.summary: The per-account device secret is never removed except on a deliberate, server-confirmed sign-out — so on a session that merely expires or a browser that is simply closed it stays in localStorage forever, contrary to the bound the design claims
samples.evidence:
`forgetDeviceSecret()` has exactly one production caller: `eraseOfflineData()` (offline-erase.ts:39). `eraseOfflineData` is reached only from (a) `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` (offline-erase.ts:332), which `api/auth.ts:134` gates on `eraseLocalData !== "none" && res?.ok`; (b) `retryPendingOfflineErase` (offline-erase.ts:368), which iterates `pendingErases()` — a list only written when an erase was *attempted and failed*; and (c) the preference-off watcher (offline-erase.ts:554). None of these fire on the 401/expiry arm (`api/auth.ts:277` passes `eraseLocalData: "none"`), nor on a browser simply being closed.

docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md states the residual is "bounded by the thirty-day sweep and by that erase's own retry". Neither bound exists in code: `WafflebaseDocStore.collectStale()` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1176) touches only IndexedDB object stores (`headers`/`snapshots`/`changes`/`archives`) and never `localStorage`, and the retry only covers erases that were already attempted.

Attack: user A works on a shared machine and their session expires (or they close the tab) rather than clicking Log out. `wafflebase-durable-device:{A}` remains in localStorage indefinitely. User B, the next person at that machine, reads it from devtools (one `localStorage.getItem` — no XSS needed), and combines it with `userId` (public in any workspace member list) and `docKey` (`sheet-<documentId>`, sitting in the URL) to reconstruct A's `wb:{secret}:{A}:{docKey}`. Per the backend's own webhook, `packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69` puts `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` in `CLIENT_METHODS` — "Methods with no document context — a valid token is sufficient" — so B can thereafter, from any machine and with only their own valid Yorkie token, deactivate or take over A's per-document client rows. Transient local access converts into a persistent remote capability against another account.
searchedFor: Grep logout across packages/frontend/src (non-test) to enumerate sign-out call sites
Read offline-erase.ts in full for every erase trigger
Read wafflebase-doc-store.ts collectStale/dropArchivesWhere/dropAllForUser for any localStorage touch
Read packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts for which Yorkie methods are document-gated

samples.summary: Keying the device secret per account does not defend against the co-located account the design names it for: localStorage is origin-scoped, so a signed-in user can read any other account's secret directly rather than deriving it
samples.evidence:
`deviceSecret(userId)` reads and writes `localStorage` at the fully predictable key `wafflebase-durable-device:{userId}` (deviceSecretKey, line 128). localStorage is partitioned by origin, never by application account, so every key in it is readable by any code running on the origin regardless of who is signed in.

The doc comment at durable-session.ts:110-124 asserts the opposite as the justification for the whole scheme: "a shared device — the case this feature exists for — is exactly where that somebody is a different person: with one value, a signed-in user could reconstruct every other account's `wb:{secret}:{userId}:{docKey}` ... One secret per account removes the shared ingredient." It does not. With per-account values, the same signed-in user obtains A's secret with `localStorage.getItem('wafflebase-durable-device:' + A)` instead of reading one shared value — the same single step. The identical claim appears in docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md ('Per account rather than per profile, because the shared device is the whole case').

The salt does genuinely defend against a *remote* workspace peer who never touches the device, which is real value — but the threat model written into the code and the design is the local one, and against that the control is ineffective. Because `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` are authorized on token validity alone (packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69), the leaked secret yields a lasting cross-account capability, not merely local read access the attacker already had.

samples.summary: A value relied on for unguessability is embedded in the Yorkie client key — an identifier transmitted on every ActivateClient, persisted server-side, and surfaced to operators/logs
samples.evidence:
`durableClientKey()` returns `wb:${deviceSecret(userId)}:${userId}:${docKey}` and this string is passed to `DurableYorkieProvider` as `clientKey` (collab-document-provider.tsx:355), which forwards it into `ClientOptions.key`. Yorkie sends that key on `ActivateClient` and stores it on the client row.

The secret's entire security purpose is that the key not be guessable — durable-session.ts:80-94 and the backend's `CLIENT_METHODS` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69, 'a valid token is sufficient') make the key the only thing standing between a workspace peer and deactivating another member's durable client. Placing that secret inside a field whose stated design purpose is the opposite — durable-session.ts:92-94 says the user and document stay in the key so as to 'make a server-side client list readable' — means the secret is written into Yorkie's client collection and into whatever request logging the deployment runs, and is exposed to anyone able to list clients for the project.

I could not confirm from this repo whether Yorkie exposes client keys to non-admin principals (no `ListClients` usage exists in packages/backend/src), so I could not complete the chain to a concrete unauthorized reader — hence low confidence. The structural problem stands regardless: a secret is being carried in an identifier field. A capability token would belong in the auth token the webhook already validates, not in the client key.

samples.summary: `randomSecret()` falls back to `Math.random()` for a value whose only job is to be unguessable
samples.evidence:
When `crypto.getRandomValues` is unavailable, the loop at durable-session.ts:143-145 fills the 8 secret bytes with `Math.floor(Math.random() * 256)`. `Math.random()` is a non-cryptographic PRNG (xorshift128+ in V8) whose internal state is recoverable from a modest number of observed outputs, so a secret minted this way is not meaningfully unguessable — and unguessability is the entire reason the salt exists (durable-session.ts:80-94).

The comment argues the branch is unreachable because `navigator.locks` and `crypto` are both secure-context APIs and `supportsDurableSession()` gates the feature on the former. That reasoning is close but not exact: `crypto.getRandomValues` is in fact available in insecure contexts in modern browsers (it is `crypto.subtle` that is secure-context-only), so the guard is really about `crypto` being absent entirely. Either way the correct handling for a security-critical secret is to refuse — return `undefined` and decline durability, the same fail-closed posture `supportsDurableSession()` already takes — rather than to mint a predictable one.

samples.summary: `collectStale()` destroys every account's archives, not just the signed-in one — the only copy of another user's unreconciled work — and this directly contradicts the design doc shipped in the same change
samples.evidence:
`collectStale` calls `this.dropArchivesWhere(BY_ARCHIVED_AT, range)` with the third parameter `onlyUser` omitted. In `dropArchivesWhere` (line 1348) that leaves `theirs === undefined`, so the `if (theirs && !theirs.has(id)) continue;` filter at line 1369 never runs and every archive row older than the cutoff is deleted regardless of its `userId`. The test added in this change asserts exactly that (`wafflebase-doc-store-cleanup.test.ts`: "collects another account's stale entries and their stale archives", expecting `theirs.listArchives()` to be `[]`).

But docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md, added in this same diff, states the opposite rule: "Archives stay scoped: another account's is the only copy of work their SDK could not reconcile, and it is theirs to collect." One principal's session is therefore silently destroying a different principal's sole copy of unsent work, on a rule the reviewed design says should not apply. `dropAllForUser` (line 1162) does pass a user-scoped index, so the capability to scope exists and is simply not used here.

Either the code or the design sentence is wrong; as shipped they disagree, which means no reviewer can tell which behaviour was intended.

samples.summary: The 403-vs-404 authorization check that makes the workspace fallback safe lives in the caller, not in the function that performs the fallback
samples.evidence:
`destinationWorkspace(given)` silently falls back to `(await fetchWorkspaces())[0].id` whenever `given` is undefined, and `recoverOfflineCopy` (lines 225 and 242) calls it unconditionally. The only thing preventing that fallback from materialising content the user may no longer read is a check in a different module: offline-runtime.tsx:271, `if (!(err instanceof HttpError) || err.status !== 404) { ...; continue; }`, plus the `reconciled` gate at offline-runtime.tsx:181.

The comment at offline-copy-recovery.ts:158-173 and at offline-runtime.tsx:254-263 both state the invariant — "only a `404` may reach that fallback" — but nothing in `recoverOfflineCopy` enforces it. `recoverOfflineCopy` is an exported function that takes `source.workspaceId?` as optional; any future caller that omits it, or any refactor that loses the 404 discrimination, silently re-enables copying an archived snapshot of a revoked workspace's document into a workspace the current user owns, with their name on it. I verified the backend distinguishes the two correctly today (`assertMember` throws `ForbiddenException`/403, `document.controller.ts:165-177`), so there is no live bypass — this is about the guard sitting outside the operation it protects.

The fix is to require the caller to state which case it observed (e.g. an explicit `sourceDeleted: true` flag) rather than inferring safety from an absent `workspaceId`.
searchedFor: Grep recoverOfflineCopy call sites across packages/frontend/src

samples.summary: `deniedIds()` fails open when the stored value parses to valid JSON that is not an array
samples.evidence:
In `deniedIds()`, a successful `JSON.parse` that yields a non-array (e.g. the literal `123` or `"abc"`) falls through the `if (Array.isArray(parsed))` branch to `return []` at line 169 — silently discarding the post-erase write denial for every account. A parse *failure* is handled more conservatively (`return [raw]`, line 167), so the two error shapes disagree about which direction is safe.

`isOfflineWritePermitted` (line 208) is the control that stops a still-mounted durable client in another tab from writing an erased account's documents back to disk after sign-out, so failing open here re-opens the exact hole the localStorage mirror was introduced to close. Reaching it requires writing to localStorage, which implies origin control, so the practical impact is small — but a security control should not fail open on an unexpected value shape.

verdict.reason: Independently verified the absence. Repo-wide grep for the storage key prefix (`wafflebase-durable-device` / `DEVICE_SECRET_PREFIX`) yields only durable-session.ts and the design doc; the only deletions are `forgetDeviceSecret` (durable-session.ts:190-197) and the explicitly test-only `resetDeviceSecretForTest` (durable-session.ts:200-218). A grep of every non-test `removeItem` and every `localStorage.clear()` in the frontend confirms no other production path clears it. `forgetDeviceSecret`'s sole production caller is `eraseOfflineData` (offline-erase.ts:39), reachable only from logout (offline-erase.ts:332, gated by api/auth.ts:134 on `eraseLocalData !== "none" && res?.ok`), the retry of already-failed erases (offline-erase.ts:368), and the preference-off watcher (offline-erase.ts:554). The 401/expiry arm explicitly passes `eraseLocalData: "none"` (api/auth.ts:277), and closing a tab runs nothing — so on expiry or tab close the secret persists indefinitely. Neither bound the code/doc claims exists: the thirty-day sweep is `store.collectStale()` (offline-runtime.tsx:123) in `wafflebase-doc-store.ts`, a file that touches no `localStorage` at all, and the retry only covers erases already attempted. The impact is the repo's own stated threat model: yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69 and 246-248 allow `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone, so a leftover salt plus the public `userId` and URL-visible `docKey` reconstructs another account's `wb:{secret}:{userId}:{docKey}` (durable-session.ts:97), converting transient local access on a shared device into a remote capability against another user's per-document client row. That is sensitive-secret retention/exposure squarely in the security lane, major severity.

finding.summary: A value relied on for unguessability is embedded in the Yorkie client key — an identifier transmitted on every ActivateClient, persisted server-side, and surfaced to operators/logs
finding.evidence:
`durableClientKey()` returns `wb:${deviceSecret(userId)}:${userId}:${docKey}` and this string is passed to `DurableYorkieProvider` as `clientKey` (collab-document-provider.tsx:355), which forwards it into `ClientOptions.key`. Yorkie sends that key on `ActivateClient` and stores it on the client row.

The secret's entire security purpose is that the key not be guessable — durable-session.ts:80-94 and the backend's `CLIENT_METHODS` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69, 'a valid token is sufficient') make the key the only thing standing between a workspace peer and deactivating another member's durable client. Placing that secret inside a field whose stated design purpose is the opposite — durable-session.ts:92-94 says the user and document stay in the key so as to 'make a server-side client list readable' — means the secret is written into Yorkie's client collection and into whatever request logging the deployment runs, and is exposed to anyone able to list clients for the project.

I could not confirm from this repo whether Yorkie exposes client keys to non-admin principals (no `ListClients` usage exists in packages/backend/src), so I could not complete the chain to a concrete unauthorized reader — hence low confidence. The structural problem stands regardless: a secret is being carried in an identifier field. A capability token would belong in the auth token the webhook already validates, not in the client key.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. durable-session.ts:96-98 returns `wb:${deviceSecret(userId)}:${userId}:${docKey}`, with deviceSecret() (lines 135-180) minting a random per-account secret whose sole documented purpose (lines 80-94, 110-117) is to make the client key unguessable. That purpose is real: yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69 defines CLIENT_METHODS = {ActivateClient, DeactivateClient} and decide() returns ALLOW for them on token validity alone (lines 245-248), with no client-key or document scoping, so the key itself is the only barrier to activating/deactivating another member's durable client row. The key is passed as clientKey at collab-document-provider.tsx:355, documented as `wb:{deviceSecret}:{userId}:{docKey}` at durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:54, and forwarded into ClientOptions.key via KeyedYorkieProvider (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:35-51, 233), so the secret is transmitted to Yorkie as the client identifier and persisted on the client row. The design comment at durable-session.ts:92-94 itself states the key is shaped to keep a server-side client list readable, which is the conflict the finding names: a bearer secret in a field intended to be readable/loggable. I found no in-repo logging of the key and no ListClients usage in packages/backend/src, but that only means I could not bound the reader set — it does not show exposure is impossible, so no refutation ground (not-present / already-guarded / out-of-scope) holds. Confidence is low because exploitability by a non-operator principal remains unproven, but the weakness and the missing server-side scoping of client-row methods are concretely in the code and in the security lane.
